A Space Probe Returns to Asteroids Where NASA Tested Planetary Defense Systems

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage.
  • Sources indicate that astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth.
  • In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “Tunguska Event,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.

Sources indicate that astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites. It will even be visible to the naked eye.

In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions. As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely key link—planetary defense technology that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.

In a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a major space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit. Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.

Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body, measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.

Sources indicate that the paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA debuted the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.

Scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet—the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.

According to recent reports, but questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars, the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.

Now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration, and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.

Recent findings suggest that but of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.

Recent findings suggest that hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an important detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface. Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.

The probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites.

Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface. Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks.

Sources indicate that according to current plans, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space. In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.

Breaking: Own Your Intelligence: A How-To Guide

📅 19 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1467 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM...
  • According to recent reports, the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM...
  • The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

According to recent reports, the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.

Recently, Alex Karp encouraged enterprises to âown the means of production.â Not long after, Satya Nadella declared that buying intelligence from a frontier lab is like paying twice: once with money, and once with the proprietary knowledge you reveal to make that intelligence useful.

The question everyone is asking: who should own the intelligence at the core of your business?

Sources indicate that to be clear, owning your intelligence is not a mandate nor a recommendation to get off the labs. For many workloads, frontier APIs and agents are still the right answer. But across our portfolio, we are seeing more companies building their own AI capabilities for parts of their products, vertically integrating toward owning and shaping their weights.

A few weeks ago, Sequoia brought together a group of AI founders and builders for an event on owning your AI stack. We had Harvey give us the customer-back view. Then Mercor, Langchain, Trajectory, and Fireworks walked us through the technical building blocks in the post-training stack.

Across the talks, a clear playbook emerged.

Industry observers note that first, the open-weight frontier has moved faster than anticipated. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are extremely good! Training on open models used to be a treadmillâ¦ you mightâve spent months fine-tuning, and the next frontier release would erase your gains. Now, you can start from a baseline close to the frontier.

Second, the independent post-training stack has matured. Thanks to companies like Mercor and Fireworks, every organization can access the technology stack of a frontier research lab, from training to inference to human or synthetic data. With strong evals, harness engineering, post-training, and online learning, open models can now beat frontier models in specific domains.

A year ago, you chose open weights when performance was something you could sacrifice. Now, it is becoming an existential and strategic question. The newest battleground is for the intelligence layer. Not your weights, not your product.

Industry observers note that thereâs no one-size-fits-all approach. In addition to performance, there may be slices of your product where renting intelligence becomes a constraint because ofâ¦.

It has been revealed that 1. Cost. The more successful your AI product, the higher your AI COGS. If inference costs scale directly with usage, owning the model is the best way to protect your margins.

Industry observers note that 2. Speed. If youâre operating in a domain like coding (tab autocomplete) or cybersecurity, a small distilled custom model might beat a large general one, because speed is so key.

Industry observers note that 3. Proprietary data. If your feedback, evals, customer interactions, or domain data are what make the system better, you might prefer that data stays within your walls.

4. Controlling your destiny. The app layer and the intelligence layer are starting to merge. The labs are moving up into product, and app companies are moving down into the training loops that define how the product thinks. Owning the product increasingly might mean controlling more of the learning loop and the intelligence itself (h/t Harvey Research, RampLabs, Glean, Factory, and more).

Recent findings suggest that assuming you've decided on your strategy for what to own vs. rent, the question becomes: how do you go from zero to one?

Build your team. Don't shoehorn this into a platform team. Owning your intelligence needs people playing offense: building evals, shaping data, experimenting with open models, tuning harnesses, and pushing performance in a domain. Small, de novo teams go very far here, partnering with half a dozen ecosystem partners. Harvey, for example, has done a surprising amount of research with a team of just seven people!

In a recent development, make the work legible. Every buyer right now is choosing their AI champion. Increasingly, the tiebreaker is published research, benchmarks, or technical posts. If you choose to do wonderful research in-house, share it with the ecosystem.

According to recent reports, execute the technical steps. Weâve laid out a high level framework below.

Harveyâs Gabe Pereyra said it well: "If you don't have a good benchmark, you can't train models.â.

In a recent development, an eval is a set of tasks that measures whether your system can do the work well. Every task contains a prompt, context the model can use, and a grader. Most evals start as a founder squinting at outputs and vibe-checking whether they feel right. The goal is to turn that judgement into something repeatable.

Harvey built its Legal Agent Benchmark by turning real legal work into discrete tasks a model could be tested on. The first iteration includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.

Itâs important to have an eval before making the decision to own your intelligence. Once every forward pass has an eval, deciding which model to use can be a measured decision instead of a guess.

2/ Harness and context engineering.

An agent has three parts: the model, the context, and the harness. The harness governs the product logic around the model: routing, retrieval, tools, memory, fallbacks, and traces. Harrison Chaseâs simple framing was that "the main job of the harness is to bring context to the model at the right point in time." The more out of distribution the task is for the model, the worse the off-the-shelf harness will be.

A good harness lets you route tasks to the best model for your specific job, reuse the same evals across models, and decide what context and tools an agent gets. It also makes the agent inspectable. You can trace what context went in, which tools were called, and where it got stuck.

Post-training covers several techniques. The right one depends on what youâre trying to improve.

Lin Qiao laid it out: if the model is missing facts, you don't need to post-train - just use context or RAG. If the output format or behavior is wrong, use supervised fine-tuning. If the issue is product taste, use preference tuning. If the model needs to improve at a specialized task, use RL. If the model is too slow or expensive, distill it.

The goal is to pick the lightest method that moves your eval. Then serve the model through the same harness and measure quality, latency, and cost as it runs.

Once the system has its pieces â evals, harness, and model â the final step is improving that system in production.

It has been revealed that arjun Karanam made a good point: models keep getting smarter, but every session feels like it's their first day on the job. You can put Terence Tao in an accounting firm, but chances are (at least on day 1) he wonât be the best accountant there. What's missing is experience, not intelligence. Agents create that experience as they run.

Recent findings suggest that A trajectory is the path through the task: the context the model saw, the tools and sub-agents it called, the answer it produced, and what the user edited, undid, or retried. Capturing those trajectories in a tool like LangChain's LangSmith is necessary to build a continuous production loop. A failed task becomes an eval. Missing information goes into context or memory. A bad tool response becomes a harness fix.

Buyer beware: owning your intelligence opens Pandoraâs box.

The closed-model stack is simple. You call a frontier model, use an out-of-the-box harness (e.g., Claude Code or Codex), add prompts and context, and ship. That gives you a high floor, but also a lower ceiling.

It has been revealed that owning your stack means taking on more of the system yourself. The production stack becomes your open-source model, custom harness, tools, and context. The development stack becomes your proprietary evals, domain data, and online learning loop.

It is certainly more work! It potentially gives you a lower floor â but it also raises the ceiling.

Industry observers note that the labs will keep building the giant brains. We should all use them.

Recent findings suggest that but, in parallel, the best product companies are growing their own little geniuses: fast, opinionated, domain-obsessed, and tuned to the work they see. In a world where more companies take ownership of their own intelligence, the ecosystem flourishes and individuality triumphs.

Thatâs the promise of a world where companies own their intelligence. And weâre delighted to see the progress from the little guys, the startups that want to bring that world into existence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.

In a recent development, most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.

Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.

According to recent reports, this is the only power bank you need. Anker combines style and substance with this versatile power bank that packs a whopping 25,000-mAh capacity and is capable of delivering up to 165 watts to two devices (100 watts for a single device connected via USB-C). I love the rounded edges, the retractable, flat 2.3-foot USB-C cable up top, and the clever braided 1-foot USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop. It has a display to show the remaining battery, charging rate in and out, battery temperature, and health. It supports pass-through charging and takes around two hours to recharge.

OK, you don’t really need this many stats, but having a precise idea of how much power remains is useful and reassuring. I love the built-in cables, because they ensure you’re never caught without one. This is also below the limit for power banks on flights, so you can travel with it. Anker’s Laptop Power Bank fast-charged everything I tested it with, including multiple smartphones, an iPad, a Poco tablet, a MacBook Air, and a Chromebook. You can charge four devices simultaneously without any concerns. After a year of use, mine still performs perfectly.

You don’t always need significant capacity, and you don’t always have room for a big power bank. If you want something more portable, go for the Nimble Champ Pro. At 6.2 ounces, it’s one of the lightest on the market. It’s smaller than a deck of cards and can deliver 20 watts to charge two devices at once via a USB-C port on either end. It feels durable, comes in a snazzy newly introduced range of speckled color finishes, and has a bright lanyard loop that makes for easy carrying and helps you pick it out of your backpack. The Pro version is bigger but doubles the capacity (to 20,000 mAh) and has a similar design with two USB-C ports that go up to 65 watts. There’s also a smaller version with a 5,200-mAh capacity that tops out at 15 watts.

Industry observers note that another reason I like Nimble is its environmental efforts. Batteries are not environmentally benign. They use lithium, cobalt, and other rare metals whose supply chains are environmentally and socially questionable at best. But Nimble’s use of bioplastics and plastic-free minimal packaging at least reduces the environmental impact where it can be reduced. This version uses 90 percent recycled plastic (up 25 percent from the original) and comes in smaller plastic-free packaging. Nimble includes a 3.3-foot USB-C to USB-C cable in the box.

Sources indicate that the original was the first Qi2 power bank I tested and was my top pick for quite a while, but this sequel is even better. The Qi2 wireless charging standard borrows elements of Apple’s MagSafe, enabling supported phones to connect with perfect alignment using a ring of magnets. Because it works with Apple's StandBy mode, you can stick Qi2 or MagSafe phones in portrait or landscape orientation.

Sources indicate that qi2 brings faster wireless charging rates of up to 25 watts, but it is also backward compatible, so older Qi devices can still charge (albeit more slowly). This compact portable charger has a handy kickstand, a two-way USB-C port on the left edge, and a power button with an LED display that can show remaining power as a percentage. It can also display charging time when plugged in, watts out, temperature, and battery health. Anker offers the device in a range of fun colors (I love the burgundy). Anker has added vents on top and bottom with a cooling fan you can turn off for silent mode. It is slimmer and lighter than the original and can charge faster, but it's also more expensive.

There are so many portable chargers out there. Here are a few more I like that just missed out on a place above for one reason or another. We also have separate guides for the Best Laptop Power Banks, Best MagSafe Power Banks, and Best Portable Power Stations.

What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

Recent findings suggest that the capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

According to recent reports, the charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no concerns. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (programmable power supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

According to recent reports, your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

Sources indicate that it’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours. If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

Recent findings suggest that some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks.

Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

It has been revealed that the chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:.

Avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most key rule. These are your most likely sources of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

Then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

It has been revealed that I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

It has been revealed that all devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when they overheat. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

According to recent reports, I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (currently an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

In a recent development, I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown fresh brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

In a recent development, there are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

I first met Mateo Jaramillo, the CEO of Form Energy, in spring 2020. It was a memorable meeting because it was the first in-person founder meeting I had in the COVID pandemic and we were all wearing masks. At that time, Mateo described a simple idea: solar and wind were going to take over the grid, but we needed batteries to store that energy. Lithium-ion was a great chemistry for cars, and it could store grid-scale energy for 4-6 hours, but it was never going to store energy for multiple days. Thinking from first principles, Mateo, who previously started and ran Teslaâs energy business, had assembled the battery Avengers, including legendary battery scientist Yet-Ming Chiang as Chief Scientist and Billy Woodford as CTO. The team set their sights on building an iron-air battery: iron, because itâs cheap and abundant, and air, because itâs free. The goal was to turn those cheap materials into a battery that could compete with gas peaker plants on cost while delivering a clean and reliable baseload energy resource.

Knowing very little about batteries at the time, I reached out to a group of professors to diligence whether the science worked. I ended up selecting a Harvard professor and hired him as a consultant. At the end of the project, he gave us a thumbs up, and as a sign of his excitement, asked if he could roll his consulting fee into our investment.

Recent findings suggest that when I arrived at Sequoia in mid-2023, Mateo was one of my first calls. At that time he was just starting construction on Form Energyâs first high-volume battery manufacturing facility, located on a shuttered steel mill site in West Virginia. I flew out for a factory visit with my partner Isaiah Boone in July 2024, and we were astounded. So many companies come to us talking about reindustrializing America, and here was a tech giant that was actually doing it, and creating more than 400 newly introduced jobs along the way. Given that China is the epicenter of battery manufacturing globally, we were energized by the potential to build a US national battery champion, starting with a fundamentally new technology, which is what America excels at.

The following year, the company went through what is colloquially termed âproduction hell.â This is exactly what Tesla, SpaceX and others had gone through before them. If you really want to reindustrialize this country, these things donât happen overnight, and they are far from easy. Companies that go through this gauntlet come out sturdier and stronger. To Mateo and the teamâs credit, they doubled down. He had by then relocated his entire family from San Francisco to Western Pennsylvania, a short drive from the plant. Having experienced this type of scaling at Tesla, Mateo knew what to do: live it, sleep it, breathe it â until you've pulled through.

And pull through he did. I knew heâd turned the corner when finally, the company received the order that everyone knew would eventually come: a large hyperscale project. Nine years in, Form had done the thing it set out to do: build battery systems that can compete with gas. In the meantime, luck worked in their favor too: AI provided a huge catalyst in the market, where suddenly rebuilding the grid went from ânice to haveâ to âneed to have.â As an AI investor, this company, which had spent years building deep relationships with utilities and regulators, was now in a prime position to serve emergent AI demand.

The opportunity to now scale up from a handful of initial projects toward completely transforming the US grid is tremendous. Not only that, but it is no longer optional â it is something that we as a country will absolutely have to do for AI to achieve its long-term potential.

The Outages Are Just Getting Started

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network.
  • So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations.
  • AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to swiftly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Industry observers note that microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed patch in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

According to recent reports, external pressures and bugs in patches are not upcoming, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

Recent findings suggest that “Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” claims Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”.

IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

It has been revealed that “AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar challenges elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”.

Sources indicate that matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

Sources indicate that there are key nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”.

Sources indicate that only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” notes Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”.

Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

Recent findings suggest that • Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some organization data. The bank notes “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

Recent findings suggest that • Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

In a recent development, spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

#23804. How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger

How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
  • The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought.
  • Recent findings suggest that the impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.

Recent findings suggest that the impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we strategy for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.

This year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” claims Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.”.

Industry observers note that el Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas—including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa—and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.

Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.

Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, claims Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”.

In a recent development, and the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, indicates Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel rolled out an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked, and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched. The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.

Recent findings suggest that as of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees Celsius—breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees Celsius—and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he says. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.

Sources indicate that unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested—though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather states.

All these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” says Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed. Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.

Sources indicate that while any year brings its own spates of bad weather—some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change—plenty of events this year have been attributed to El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the Peruvian anchovy fishery, which was closed dramatically early this year to give anchovies a fighting chance in the face of warm waters and less plankton, one of their main food sources. This industry, typically worth between $2 billion and $3 billion, is a huge contributor to global feed for livestock and aquaculture. As of September, global fishmeal output was about half what it was the year before; fishmeal prices have spiked, with some European salmon farmers turning to cheaper chicken byproducts.

In a recent development, in Indonesia, palm oil mills stopped buying fruit from farmers because an ongoing drought shriveled the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River. In Cambodia, a delayed rainy season is drying out rice fields. Panama has declared a national state of emergency (as it did for the 2023 and 2015 El Niños), and the Panama Canal is carrying less ship traffic and transporting less food in the face of dwindling rainfall. In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock from March to August next year. El Niño-induced drought alongside record summer temperatures in Central America has eaten away at crop yields and threatens that region’s second planting cycle: The E.U.’s Joint Research Centre projects an 83 percent spike in people suffering from acute food insecurity in that area.

Perhaps surprisingly, the global food production outlook for this growing season isn’t as bad as one might think: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) notes that the USDA projects worldwide production of maize, wheat, and rice for 2026-2027 to be just 2.7 percent below the previous year’s production, which will still make it the second-largest annual crop on record.

“Globally, food supply is not of high concern,” says FEWS NET advisor Amy Ostrander. “The concerns are production changes in some specific regions, such as Southern Africa, and food access.” Even if sufficient crops are harvested in those regions, in other words, some food won’t make it to market, and some people won’t be able to afford it.

An analysis by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization concludes that the highest risks from El Niño–prompted droughts will be in the Sahel, Southern Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and in Central America’s Dry Corridor and the Caribbean.

One good thing about an El Niño is that meteorologists can see it coming almost a year in advance, unlike freak weather events, which are harder to forecast. This gives agencies a fighting chance to protect people by distributing drought-resistant seeds, for example, securing deals for future emergency food supplies and transport, or setting up income assistance for struggling farmers.

The World Food Programme first tested its forecast-based financing program in Zimbabwe during the 2015 El Niño: Delivering cash to families in one district facing drought helped them to sustain their quantity and quality of food, while a neighboring district that didn’t receive cash aid saw a massive drop. This year, the WFP has been delivering cash and other assistance, including, for example, more than 3,000 airtight silos for farmers in Guatemala to help them safely store grain. As of October, the program indicates it has reached 28 million people across 15 countries with early warning information and assistance.

Recent findings suggest that cash is strapped for such programs, though. Funds for global aid were down 30 percent in 2025 from their 2022 peak and are still falling, making it hard for the WFP and others to do their work. In Somalia, the WFP helped 10 million people during a drought in 2022; today, in the face of similar conditions, notes Choularton, they can afford to reach fewer than a million.

Advanced warning is good, says Lobell, but challenges will still abound, and even harder times may lie ahead as El Niños pile on top of climate change. The peaks of strong El Niños are almost always followed by record-breaking years for the global average temperature. The anomalously hot years of 1998, 2016, and 2024 (the current record holder) all followed hot on the heels of El Niño peaks the year before. While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says Hausfather.

It has been revealed that global warming, of course, also has impacts on food supply. Last year, Lobell published a paper showing that total wheat, barley, maize, rice, and soybean yields are now altogether about 5 percent lower overall than they would have been in a world without climate change. “To a lot of people, that sounds like a small number. But the kind of shocks that we talk about can be far smaller than that,” he indicates. “It doesn’t take much of a supply shift to have an important effect on people’s lives.”.

According to recent reports, because the specific places that get warmer and drier during El Niños are different from the specific places that get warmer and drier from climate change, researchers caution that what we see in 2026 won’t be a precise forerunner of things to come. But how we deal with this temporary challenge does say something about the resilience of our food systems, says Lobell, and it will reveal how we might cope in the future with other climate disruptions to crops. “That’s one of the massive questions,” he says. “How much can you adapt when the conditions are bad?”.

Change has always been the fundamental operational signal in infrastructure. Empirik is turning that signal into the foundation for autonomous, agentic infrastructure engineering.

Recent findings suggest that this one started close to home. Before Sequoia, our Chief Digital and Information Officer, Avon Puri, had spent two decades running IT and infrastructure at scale as SVP & CIO at Rubrik, and VP of Engineering and Applications at VMware (also my alma mater in the tech world). Avon and Sudheer Dhurjati, who worked alongside him at all three companies, watched the same story repeat: enterprise infrastructure operates in a reactive posture. Companies spend tens of billions of dollars on observabilityâmetrics, logs, and tracesâto tell us when a system is failing. But traditional observability is inherently post-mortem.

The real driver of infrastructure behavior is change: a upcoming identity policy is attached, a new Terraform provider completes, or a feature flag flips in production. However, change has been treated as an administrative process constraint, a static ticket, an approval form, or as tribal knowledge buried in email or Slack. It was sometimes recorded for compliance, but never truly put to work to do actual infrastructure engineering jobs.

Recent findings suggest that if you understand the real-time stream of changes across every layer of the environment, you don't just get better alertsâyou unlock true autonomy. Every change reflects an engineer's intent; once a system can interpret that intent and assess its impact, it can decide whether to act on its own or loop in a human. By bringing agentic capabilities to infrastructure, you solve the full lifecycle of infrastructure engineering jobs, shifting from a reactive firefighting posture to a proactive one.

It has been revealed that that insight became the founding pillar behind Empirik. Avon and Sudheer built the initial version inside Sequoia. We saw companies rushing to deploy AI agents to automate coding, marketing, and many other enterprise processes, but infrastructure was the one place nobody was modernizing. After the same rigorous evaluation any other Sequoia investment goes through, Empirik spun out as an independent organization. And now, itâs under the leadership of CEO Kartik Chandrayana, a repeat founder who sold his first company, Twin Prime, to Salesforce, then spent five years as Salesforce's VP of Product for Observability and Massive Data, and most recently was CPO at Quantum Metric. Today, we're excited to share that Empirik is emerging from stealth with $21M in funding.

Agentic coding has taken off because code lives in version-controlled repositories that make a system's architecture and intent legible to a model. Infrastructure has never had that foundation. Infrastructure-as-code is a good start, but because it represents a declared state and not what's actually running in production, it's inherently behind. There's no unified, real-time representation of an organization's infrastructure across the maze of cloud resources, Kubernetes, networking, identity, and legacy systems. Infrastructure does not have the notion of a pull request; instead, every change still runs through tribal knowledge and institutional memory of people rather than the machine rigor of software.

Industry observers note that observability is already a large, proven marketâDatadog, Dynatrace, and Splunk are behemoths with billions in revenue. But all of observability is built to measure symptoms: latency spiked, errors climbed, a pod crashed. Empirik's bet is that there's a fourth pillar hiding in plain sightâthe changes themselves. Instead of "latency in service X increased 300% in the last 24 hours," Empirik tells you, "Joe deployed a Terraform provider that shut down three VMs in AWS"âthe actual cause and context, not just the symptom. And why stop there? With Empirik, you can actually warn or stop Joe even before he deploys Terraform because Empirik computes that risk at the inception of change.

In a recent development, as Kartik describes it: infrastructure today is where software engineering was three years agoâbefore Claude Code and Cursor, when every action needed a human in the loop because there was no reliable map of the system to reason over. Empirik is building that map, and putting it to work as the Autonomous Infra EngineerâAI that can safely initiative, reason about, and operate enterprise infrastructure. It's already plugged into agentic workflows via MCP, connecting directly into tools like Claude and ChatGPT, so that humans and agents alike can reason over infrastructure change with real contextânot guesswork.

Industry observers note that under the hood is an infrastructure compiler. Just as a traditional compiler translates source code into executable software, Empirik converts metadata from a customerâs clouds, identity providers, CI/CD, and SaaS systems into a live, unified operational graphâmapping thousands of relationships between assets and accounts. That graph is how the product knows, in real time, what changed, who changed it, and whether itâs the reason something broke.

In a recent development, what I particularly appreciate about the teamâs approach is that they didnât take shortcuts. Itâs easy for modern startups to build exclusively for greenfield Kubernetes or a single public cloud provider. But from day one, Avon, Sudheer, and Kartik designed Empirik for the reality of the Fortune 500 enterprise: a complex, multi-decade hybrid stack spanning public clouds, legacy on-prem infrastructure, identity layers, and critical SaaS apps. An infrastructure graph that only sees half your environment misses the mark for an enterprise buyer. Empirikâs graph connects the entire surface area so teams and agents have complete operational context.

The traction backs up the thesis. Fortune500 Financial enterpriseâs interest in the product traces directly back to a P0 outage caused by an unapproved change. TCBPay, a payment processing organization with $1.5B+ in annual volume now catches sensitive config file changes in 10 seconds, down from 30 minutes. Avahi, an MSP, integrated Empirik within their GitHub Actions to evaluate and block risky changes at the source. Guardant Health found Empirik so valuable that it expanded its deployment from production to all dev environments, and even expanded to on-prem. And a global Fortune-50 CPG company is also expanding its footprint, relying on Empirik to drive most of its agentic and autonomous infra roadmap. Empirik is now processing millions of raw change and telemetry events every week, over dependency graphs spanning a few million resources across all major clouds and on-prem systems. Customers are reporting benefits in multiple domains: preventing risky changes from making it to production, detecting unapproved changes, faster incident response, making rollback decisions, and detecting drifts, among others.

It has been revealed that the success is no surprise given this team. Avon and Sudheer are two of the best operators we know, and they built Empirik the way they'd have wanted it built for themselves. Kartik, meanwhile, has firsthand expertise in shipping observability products at enterprise scale. Most enterprises still can't answer that simple but critical question: what changed, and did that cause the incident? Empirik is building the system of record for that questionâfor humans today, and for the agents that will increasingly be making those changes themselves tomorrow.

#23801. Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1725 w)

Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
  • For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt.
  • They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration—to drop.

They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.

According to recent reports, fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.

In a recent development, now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances, they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules, may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine said.

In a recent development, the experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” said Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life, he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology.”.

Recent findings suggest that when he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes, the carbon emission rate declined quickly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.

When he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.

Industry observers note that convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences. Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.

They considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.

It has been revealed that through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining showed no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination, the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.

By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.

For six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.

When they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples indicated higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.

During metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.

In a recent development, he devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.

In a recent development, it was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv.org, Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.

According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.

For Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he remarked. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.

Recent findings suggest that the idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his, suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.

“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran said.

Cell-free metabolic reactions could be more common than previously thought and don’t need special conditions to get started, said Markus Ralser, a biochemist at Charité University Hospital in Berlin, who found some of the first enzyme-free metabolic reactions.

“This fits a bit into my thinking about how metabolism started in evolution,” he noted of the upcoming work. “If it would be very hard to do, then the planet would not be full of life now.” This idea is complicated, however, by the low-oxygen conditions in which life arose.

According to recent reports, another explanation for the observed results could be that enzymes, loosed from the irradiated cells, might be hanging around in the soil and continuing their biochemical jobs. Even when degraded, enzymes have stable backbones that might be capable of catalyzing reactions, remarked Sudha Rajamani, an astrobiologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Pune who wasn’t involved in the study.

Industry observers note that ralser agrees with her. “My gut feeling is they still have a lot of enzymes there [in Fontaine’s irradiated soil], even after six years,” he remarked. To know whether metals and minerals in soil could spontaneously carry out these reactions, the researchers would have to eliminate enzymes from the mixture. But that’s really hard: They would have to get the soil so hot that it would damage the soil structure itself.

However, the activity of such enzymes diminishes “exponentially” after they spill out of cells, Bouquet remarked. Plus, no enzyme is known to last six years, Fontaine added. He doesn’t doubt that enzymes released by living and recently dead cells contribute to carbon emissions in real-world soils, but the long-term experimental results make it “very unlikely that the respiration we observed is due to enzymes,” he said.

For Bouquet, chasing this years-long obsession has highlighted that “even in a context as close and familiar to us as terrestrial soil, we are not always able to distinguish or recognize processes that indicate the presence or absence of living organisms.” Now a researcher at the Collège de France and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, he is looking for prebiotic origins of other biochemical cascades.

“I find it particularly interesting to imagine the survival of processes that may predate life itself,” Bouquet stated, “right there under our feet.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that every agent now imports plugins and skills from random places.
  • We met Yair Saban and Niv Hoffman before they had a company, a name, or a product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every agent now imports plugins and skills from random places. Yair and Niv are building the software supply chain defenses for AI.

Recent findings suggest that every agent now imports plugins and skills from random places. Yair and Niv are building the software supply chain defenses for AI.

We met Yair Saban and Niv Hoffman before they had a company, a name, or a product. But as we ran our references on them across the Israeli cybersecurity ecosystem, the same answer kept coming back: they would be among the strongest founding teams in the country. One of the former commanders of Unit 8200 told us Yair was "the only person I have ever thought had everything required to one day command Unit 8200" â about as strong an endorsement as exists in Israeli tech. Niv is a technical outlier who led 8200âs most notable vulnerability research department, building a network of elite technical talent. Yair finished his service on a Thursday, and we shook hands on a seed investment that Saturday, which tells you all you need to know about the pace at which this team operates.

It has been revealed that well before Yair and Niv started building a defensive security product, they built MOAK, the "Mother of All KEVs," an agentic workflow that produces working exploits for freshly published vulnerabilities with no human in the loop. In one demonstration, MOAK exploited a React vulnerability in 21 minutes, versus the six days or so it takes a typical enterprise to roll out a patch. They released it publicly, to ring an alarm bell that the industry was badly underestimating the leverage attackers can now get from AI, and that defensive tooling needed to catch up.

Recent findings suggest that the day developers started importing other people's packages instead of writing everything themselves, software acquired a supply chain. It then took two decades and a number of painful incidents, from log4j to Solarwinds, to build the machinery for inspecting what was coming in. Agents now have precisely the same problem, except that their supply chain is assembled at runtime and often nobody is inspecting it at all. An enterprise agent consumes skills, plugins, MCP servers, sub-agents, hooks, commands and rules â each running with the agentâs own permissions, inside a userâs environment, against a userâs data. Usually, theyâre installed with the care most of us would give a browser extension.

Air has spent the past several months demonstrating the stakes. They wrote a deliberately malicious skill and watched multiple AI marketplaces wave it through as safe. Their Story of Skills research revealed a researcher-built malicious skill reaching more than 26,000 agents through a trusted marketplace and social media, with every scanner clearing it. Then they published SkillJacking, which showed 925 live skills were pulling their dependencies and prompts from dead links; Air registered those links and took control of the roughly 134,000 agents that had installed them. Every public scanner they tested missed the problems completely.

The same day, Yair and Niv shipped ScanAir, an OWASP-aligned scanner for agentic skills. That sequence â find the hole, prove it, publish it, then ship the thing that closes it â is the pattern we like most about this team.

Today, Air has three products that between them cover the full lifecycle of an agent's add-ons. Air Filter vets every add-on before an agent is permitted to consume it, using static analysis, dependency checks and sandbox detonation. It then intercepts unsafe installations in real time and offers safe alternatives in their place. Air Defend monitors what agents actually do once theyâre running and provides security operations teams with detection and response capabilities for agent behavior. Finally, Air Control handles posture and policy, from knowing which agents exist and what theyâre allowed to touch, to revoking a bad skill across thousands of agents at once. Think of it like home security: Air Filter is the locks and the childproofing, Air Defend is the cameras and the person watching them, and Air Control is the panel by the door â every entry point accounted for, every code assigned, and all of them revocable at once.

Every couple of years, the best cyber talent coming out of Unit 8200 consolidates around a handful of teams. First it was Wiz, Cyera, and, Island; then it was Eon, Glow, Decart, and Kela; now it is Air. Yair and Niv are smart, hungry natural leaders who have proven their ability to attract extreme talent density; in only a few short months they have built a cracked team of the very best. We at Sequoia are proud to led their seed round, and to now double down in their Series A.

It has been revealed that as enterprises move toward handing agents real authority over real systems, every CISO will be asked the same questions: what is our agent actually running, where did it come from, and who checked it? Today, few have complete answers. But Air is building the system of record that will.

#23799. Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (927 w)
