📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

Josh and Jason are building the data and deployment layer for physical AI.

AI took the digital world by storm in a few short years, and we are still only scratching the surface. Each time digital AI has moved to a latest phase, from pretraining to reinforcement learning to deployment, spend on compute and data has not plateaued. It has accelerated.

Recent findings suggest that bringing AI into the physical world will be a wave of comparable importance to digital AI, if not larger, but the infrastructure required to get there will be harder to build and scale, and that already shows at every stage. In pretraining, language models benefited from decades of text accumulated on the internet. Robotics has no comparable, ready-made collection of the movements, interactions and sensory information needed to understand the physical world. That experience has to be captured before it can be learned from. In reinforcement learning and deployment, digital AI operates in clean, structured environments that are easy to scale. Physical AI lives in the noisy, unpredictable, operationally complex reality of the real world. It operates in the field, not in the cloud.

To reach physical AGI, the industry has to build both the brain and the body. The brain needs data that wasnât collected. The body needs someone doing the work on the ground.

That is the mission Josh, Jason and the Mecka AI team have taken on: helping physical AI labs, robotics companies and end enterprises reach physical AGI and put it to use, by being their partner for training data, reinforcement learning, and deployment.

Delivering on this mission requires developing several muscles across disciplines, all at once and all at scale:.

Research: Identify the next wave in robotics, and what it will require, before it arrives.

Hardware: Once you see the wave, design the bespoke hardware and wearables to capture the data, then manufacture them fast, economically, and at scale.

Sources indicate that operations: Run large-scale global operations to collect the data. Volume alone is not enough; the data has to span every job in every industry.

Software and digital AI: Turn the raw output, which is far more voluminous and complex than text (e.g., multi-camera video, body and hand tracking, sensor streams), into high-quality, training-ready data.

Deployment: Put robots in front of end customers, for reinforcement learning and production deployment.

Recent findings suggest that each of these muscles is difficult to develop on its own, but to win, you need not one but all of them, working together and at scale. Training data today, for example, has to be high volume AND high diversity AND high quality AND delivered fast AND at a good price. It is easy to do one of these at small volume, but it is incredibly difficult to do all of them at once and at scale, and that is what it takes to help partners reach physical AGI. In the same way, it is easy to start a food delivery business that delivers a single dish from one restaurant to one apartment block, but it is incredibly difficult to scale it into a DoorDash.

Mecka's founders and team understood this and moved fast to build all five muscles, finding differentiated edge in each and executing on it. The result is a strong, scalable and flexible platform that has enabled them to win over many of the leading AI labs and robotics companies and promptly become the emerging leader of this category.

What drew us to Mecka is not that they made the right bet on the right form of data (although they did). Robotics is still early relative to digital AI. The form factor of the data might change. The form factor of the robots might change. What matters is that they built the machine that scales with the industry and its partners; regardless of how the input changes over time, the output will be what their partners want. In the same way, DoorDash built a system where, whether the input is a pizza or a laptop, the customer gets the same delightful delivery experience. And when something in the physical world has high barriers to scale, it is an opportunity for the right team to build a large, durable business with moats.

That is why we are excited to back Josh, Jason and their fast-growing team. We see in them the special ingredients that will keep compounding over the long term to win this category and help their partners advance the mission of building and deploying robots at scale around the world.

And it is why others have joined us, from strategics like NVIDIA, Samsung, Microsoft and Qualcomm to the founders and operators who scaled some of the most defining companies of their generation and excel in many of the disciplines required in Meckaâs business: Tony Xu, founder and CEO of DoorDash; Frank Slootman, former CEO of ServiceNow and Snowflake; Milan Kovac, former head of Optimus at Tesla; Christopher Payne, former President & COO of Doordash; Jonathan Chadwick, former COO and CFO of VMware and board member at Databricks; and many more.Photo by S72 Business Portraits.

What if machine intelligence were as dependable as a database query?

What if machine intelligence were as dependable as a database query?

If models have reached superhuman intelligence, where is all the automation?

The ChatGPT moment put AI front and center in the consumer mind. Claude Code transformed the life of the individual developer. With the âJev moment,â TypeSafe is going after the next paradigm: models that power software at runtime, making zillions of decisions with no humans in the loop.

The early response has been extraordinary. Within 24 hours of launch on September 15, TypeSafeâs first model, Jev, became the fastest-adopted model in Vercelâs AI Gateway history. Over the past few weeks, weâve heard from many of our portfolio companies, who are racing to put it into production for a myriad of upcoming use cases. It is the type of developer pull we havenât seen since GPT-3.

Jev flips the LLM on its head. Rather than writing out an answer word by word, it takes in context and a set of questions and returns typed answers with confidence scores, all at once. If LLMs are AIâs System 2, slow and deliberate, Jev is System 1: cheap, fast, intuitive and built for the thousands of small judgment calls software makes every second.

Thereâs so much you can do with Jev. Decide which button an agent should click next. Grade evals, route requests, triage tickets, pull fields out of contracts. Jev offers the kind of out-of-the-box generality that feels like magic, with no labeled data or training team required. Developers are finding new use cases every day, from playing Doom, to re-ranking their news feeds, to generating Super Mario multiverses.

Jev is named after Jevons paradox: when something gets dramatically cheaper, we use far more of it. TypeSafe is betting the same will be true of intelligence.

When classification is expensive, teams ration it. They grade a sample of agent runs rather than all of them, define brittle rules instead of calling on a model, or ask one broad question instead of ten specific ones. When classification is nearly free, those tradeoffs go away.

That changes what is worth building. Many of the world's problems are Jev-shaped, which is obvious from the explosion of volume and creativity in use cases that folks are discovering. We think itâs likely that the most vital things to be built on Jev havenât even been imagined yet.

Sources indicate that diogo Almeida first got the idea for TypeSafe while working on InstructGPT and RLHF at OpenAI. Models were being trained to be wonderful conversational partners â great for human interaction and human-in-the-loop. But, real automation needed something different: AI that is reliable, fast, and cheap. His conclusion, which he calls the âbitterest lesson,â was that picking the right task to solve matters even more than scale.

Born in the Philippines and a *top 30* North American League of Legends player, Diogo is a rare mix: an iconoclastic, creative researcher with real developer taste and commercial instinct. He is wildly ambitious and refreshingly pragmatic, which is exactly what is needed to usher in the next machine age.

Jev has captured lightning in a bottle, but it is only the opening salvo. TypeSafe wants to become the infrastructure layer for how software makes decisions: a platform of primitives developers can compose and build on, the way they once built on databases.

We are absolutely thrilled to be partnering with Diogo, co-founders Sasha Sheng and Erik Spock Gafni, and the TypeSafe team in their Series A, behind our friends at a16z.

Breaking: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (433 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company.
  • Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
  • Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game blueprint to hold them long term. In just the last year, the manufacturer has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

Latest Update: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit.
  • The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
  • Recent findings suggest that those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?

The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

Recent findings suggest that those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the firm’s orbital data center prepares. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

That may not matter to the organization in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

It has been revealed that however, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the firm failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

It has been revealed that even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

According to recent reports, that might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks.
  • Sources indicate that the broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public.
  • Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.

Sources indicate that the broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.

Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.

An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.

The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.

Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.

Industry observers note that google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the firm’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.

XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.

Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the manufacturer will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.

Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.

The startup’s newly confirmed technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.

In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.

Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.

As with any upcoming technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO2-cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.

That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.

JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.

JP, Aayush and Maru are building infrastructure for developers to validate and ship trustworthy code as fast as agents can write it.

Sources indicate that software development has a new bottleneck. Writing code is no longer the hard part; trusting it is. Coding agents now produce more code than any team can read or any existing system can verify. Led by co-founders Aditya Jayaprakash (JP), Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, Blacksmith is building infrastructure that can.

In a recent development, last month, Anthropicâs engineering team described what happened as their own usage of coding agents scaled. Engineers began shipping roughly eight times as much code per quarter. Their test suite grew tenfold. The volume of continuous integration (CI) jobs, the builds and tests that check every change before it reaches production, grew 25x in six months. Anthropic is very far along the curve, but is on the same curve as every tech giant, and its advice to the rest of the industry was to plan for 25x the CI load within two quarters.

For decades, software development scaled as a function of engineering capacity. Developers were the scarce resource. Shipping more meant hiring more. That has changed. Developers now direct fleets of coding agents that work in parallel, around the clock and increasingly autonomously. These agents do not produce finished work. They produce attemptsâa patch, a test, a migration, a throwaway branchâeach iterating against a test suite until it is ready to merge. Meanwhile, the quiet backbone of software development that validates and tests code has not changed.

Validating code has also never been more vital. AI coding tasks produce large volumes of security flaws, and the same model capabilities that write the code now make those flaws more dangerous. The system that was supposed to catch them is straining right as developers need it the most. With the scale and velocity of this shift, the constraint in software has moved from writing code to proving it works and is safe.

In a recent development, this is the problem Blacksmith set out to solve. The team started with speeding up CI. With a one-line change in a workflow file, developers using Blacksmith see their CI jobs complete twice as fast and at 60% lower cost on average. Underneath a simple product experience is a stack purpose-built from the bare metal up, designed to absorb demand spikes from customers and get faster and more efficient as it scales.

In a recent development, developers have noticed. The business has seen explosive growth this year. More than 10,000 companies are using Blacksmith, up from 700 a year ago. Weekly CI jobs are up 18x, from 5 million to 90 million, in 2026 alone. And ARR has grown 17x over the same time period, with the largest customers now spending more than $1M per year.

Recent findings suggest that much of our conviction in Blacksmith is driven by the team behind it. Co-founders JP, Aayush and Maru have known each other since their undergraduate years at the University of Waterloo, and developed a maniacal focus on hyper-performant systems at Cockroach Labs and Faire. They founded Blacksmith in 2024, as autocomplete was giving way to coding assistants, on the conviction that the volume of code needing to be tested would go up by orders of magnitude. For the rest of the world, the future became clear in 2026 with the arrival of truly autonomous coding agents, but Blacksmith had already been building for it. The Blacksmith team is talent-dense and is growing rapidly. The roadmap is exciting, with several debuts planned in the coming months.

According to recent reports, we are proud to lead Blacksmithâs Series C. The world is about to run far more code than it has ever written, and someone has to make sure it works. We look forward to supporting JP, Aayush and Maru as they build infrastructure that runs at agent speed, in validation and beyond.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s a massive week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab.
  • “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
  • The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s a massive week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

Sources indicate that maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this ….

The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.

For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”.

However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another notable proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”.

Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.

Recent findings suggest that in a brief introduction to his proof, which he stated is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”.

This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
  • The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer.
  • Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Recent findings suggest that pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in Upcoming Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”.

#23771. Tech Report: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (930 w)

Tech Report: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.
  • “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.
  • That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

Sources indicate that but now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”.

According to recent reports, huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of tech giant secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

Recent findings suggest that and typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Recent findings suggest that honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown mentioned. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”.

What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a initiative. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

Recent findings suggest that “AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”.

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.

It has been revealed that “Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”.

Carpenter mentioned a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

According to recent reports, bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown mentioned. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”.

It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the firm.

Recent findings suggest that brown added that tech giant culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that “Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown noted. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets owners share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.
  • GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.
  • Industry observers note that santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets owners share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.

GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.

Industry observers note that santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The tech giant also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.

It has been revealed that in its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The firm debuted StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024.

Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1.

“We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing.

Industry observers note that in the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale.

Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android.

Apple did not respond to a request for comment.

Industry observers note that india has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino manufacturer has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth.

Latest Update: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office.
  • Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska, making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959.
  • Sources indicate that on a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska, making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.

Sources indicate that on a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains.

Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most notable sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.

Sources indicate that “The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.

Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.

So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more crucial messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.

“Ha, yes, that’s me,” he replied.

So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

#23766. Industry News: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1360 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry.
  • Industry observers note that the primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions.
  • Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The firm produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.

Industry observers note that the primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.

Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”.

Lately, however, the organization’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.

Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.

The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.

This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.

In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a latest era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”.

Industry observers note that guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni mentioned. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”.

But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?

Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the firm’s website appear to have millions of views.

Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a latest generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.

A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”.

It has been revealed that much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”.

Recent findings suggest that how much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The tech giant isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.

A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the manufacturer didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person stated, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”.

According to recent reports, for other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.

Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.

Industry observers note that “Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”.

Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its latest face-licensing endeavor.

Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators team up with a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a manufacturer called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.

Industry observers note that cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she states. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”.

Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she stated, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
  • You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf.
  • While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.

While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.

Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the tech giant explains on its website.

According to recent reports, it works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.

Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a newly introduced activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.

There’s also a work-focused version, which the tech giant explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”.

According to recent reports, the personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.

Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.

In a recent development, caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone owners and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

It has been revealed that for instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.

Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

In a recent development, comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.

Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.

According to recent reports, it can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.

Comma is free to start and open source.

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

Recent findings suggest that the service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.

Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.

Sources indicate that the firm introduced in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.

Industry observers note that one distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.

Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.

Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.

According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”.

Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.

Industry observers note that presently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.

Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.

It has been revealed that the always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Consumers can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The firm says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.

The manufacturer remains in private beta.

Recent findings suggest that powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.

Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of customers by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.

It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.

Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.

Sources indicate that it can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.

The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use.

It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month,  20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.

Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. People can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.

Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

It has been revealed that owners can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.

It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

It has been revealed that it works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.

Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.

Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.

Sources indicate that users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of intends, receipts, dates, files, and other details.

There’s a free initiative available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.

According to recent reports, poke debuted in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent organization The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.

Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.

Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

It has been revealed that instead of waiting for customers to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet declared a public release date.

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Consumers can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and strategy from scratch.

Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Owners can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.

According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.

Industry observers note that tab allows users to delegate everyday tasks through familiar messaging platforms. Users can send requests to the assistant via iMessage or WhatsApp, ranging from ordering groceries to finding birthday gifts, and Tab handles the process on their behalf.

The company emerged from stealth in early October with a valuation of $300 million. Its investors include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.

The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.

The basic strategy starts at $19.99 per month.

Sources indicate that town is aimed more at professional life. It gives owners a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms.

In June 2026, the firm raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.

Recent findings suggest that underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that debuted an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

The organization aims to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

It has been revealed that A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring owners to hand over their own credentials.

Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo notes it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.

Fo launched publicly in September 2026 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI agents will ask far more questions of a company's data than people ever did.
  • In a recent development, AI agents will ask far more questions of a organization's data than people ever did.
  • Last fall we got a message from Roy Reznik, one of the co-founders of Wiz, offering to introduce us to a team that had just left Microsoft.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AI agents will ask far more questions of a company's data than people ever did. Edelbyte is building the data platform that can answer all of them, fast and at a price that makes sense.

In a recent development, AI agents will ask far more questions of a organization's data than people ever did. Edelbyte is building the data platform that can answer all of them, fast and at a price that makes sense.

Last fall we got a message from Roy Reznik, one of the co-founders of Wiz, offering to introduce us to a team that had just left Microsoft. This was the only introduction to a founding team weâd ever received from Roy, and we paid attention.

The people Roy wanted us to meet had built Kusto, a data engine that started more than a decade ago as a small incubation project inside Microsoft. Named after the oceanographer Jacques Cousteau because it was built for diving into oceans of data, Kusto was designed to get answers from enormous volumes of fast-arriving data, such as logs, telemetry and security events, in seconds rather than hours. It ran on a query language simple enough that anyone, not just significant-data engineers, could use it. And it worked so well that it became the data engine underneath Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft Defender and Azure Monitor, and was eventually offered to customers as Azure Data Explorer. Security teams in particular loved it, which is how Roy became one of its biggest champions. When we spoke with customers, large enterprises and fast-growing startups alike told us two things: it was game-changing data technology, and the team behind it was among the best theyâd ever worked with.

It has been revealed that avner Aharoni, Evgeney Ryzhyk, Alexander Sloutsky and Yoni Leibowitz were that team. Evgeney invented the Kusto engine and its query language, then rebuilt it three times, making it faster and cheaper with each iteration. Alexander turned half-formed ideas into finished features seemingly overnight, and Yoni made sure every complex design was fully thought through, starting before a line of code was ever written. Avner, who spent a quarter century at Microsoft, hustled Kusto from project to a globally beloved product. Their fresh company, Edelbyte, builds on this success. We are proud to have led their seed round and to be their partners.

In a recent development, in B2B technology, this is a proven playbook: a team develops a solution inside a large tech giant and then splits off to build it independently. Itâs the origin story of Sequoia portfolio companies such as Confluent, whose founders created Kafka at LinkedIn, and Temporal, whose founders built Cadence at Uber. Edelbyte now follows the same path.

According to recent reports, but Edelbyte is not simply Kusto rebuilt for a fourth time; it is a rethinking, from first principles, of what a data platform should look like in the age of AI. With every major shift in computing, the way software is built changes, and the data infrastructure underneath it has to change too. Data platforms were designed around human customers, and there is a natural limit on the number of questions one person can type in a day. That made the trade-offs, such as keeping less history so queries stay fast, asking fewer questions so the bill stays reasonable, and building the product inside whichever cloud the database happens to run in, easier to tolerate.

In a recent development, but an AI agent investigating a problem is like a whole team of curious analysts who never get tired, testing multiple hypotheses concurrently. One agent might fire off fifty queries where a person would run one. And at that scale, rationing and trade-offs quickly constrain the true promise of AI. An agent is only as useful as the questions it can afford to ask, and what it can afford is decided in the data layer.

Sources indicate that edelbyte keeps detailed history queryable at interactive speed, scales as data volumes and query demand grow, and gives people, applications and AI agents governed access to the same data. It brings search and analytics, which have historically been stitched together from separate systems at significant cost and complexity, together in a single platform. And it runs wherever you need it: in the cloud or on premises, managed or self-hosted.

The result is exactly what an AI-heavy workload needs: no more rationing curiosity, whether it comes from a person or an agent. Already, customers are seeing dramatic increases in efficiency, including tenfold increases in queries with no increase in budget.

Data platforms are among the most durable and lucrative businesses in technology, because data has gravity; once it accumulates in one place it rarely moves. Each era produces its own winners, and we believe the AI era will be won by the platform that lets builders, and the agents working for them, ask as many questions as they want without worrying about the speed or the bill. Edelbyte is building just such a platform, and we are thrilled to be part of the journey.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to reports in CNN and the Associated Press.

The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more. The scope of the breach does not yet appear to be clear.

A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an problem, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”.

President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also noted that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”.

In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack.
